q: How many base units does the SI system have?
x: The SI has seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Six is the usual slip of forgetting the candela or the mole.

q: Which of the following is a derived SI unit?
x: The coulomb is defined from base units as 1 C = 1 A s, so it is derived. The ampere, kelvin and candela are all base units; the ampere is tempting because charge and current are linked.

q: A living cell has a volume of 1000 μm³. Its volume in cubic metres is:
x: 1 μm³ = (10⁻⁶ m)³ = 10⁻¹⁸ m³, so 1000 μm³ = 10³ × 10⁻¹⁸ = 10⁻¹⁵ m³. Using 10⁻⁶ without cubing gives 10⁻³ m³; forgetting the 1000 gives 10⁻¹⁸ m³.

q: A pressure is given as 5 N cm⁻². In pascals (N m⁻²) this is:
x: 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², so 5 N cm⁻² = 5 N / 10⁻⁴ m² = 5 × 10⁴ Pa. Converting cm to m without squaring gives 5 × 10² Pa; multiplying by 10⁻⁴ instead of dividing gives 5 × 10⁻⁴ Pa.

q: A light pulse travels 6 × 10⁴ m in 2 × 10⁻⁴ s. Its speed is:
x: Speed = (6 × 10⁴)/(2 × 10⁻⁴) = 3 × 10⁴⁻⁽⁻⁴⁾ = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Adding the exponents instead of subtracting gives 3 × 10⁰; multiplying the numbers gives 1.2 × 10¹.

q: A tap delivers water at 36 litres per minute. In SI units this flow rate is:
x: 36 L = 36 × 10⁻³ m³ = 3.6 × 10⁻² m³, and 1 min = 60 s, so the rate is 3.6 × 10⁻²/60 = 6 × 10⁻⁴ m³ s⁻¹. Treating a litre as 1 m³ gives 6 × 10⁻¹; taking 1 L = 10⁻⁶ m³ (a cm³) gives 6 × 10⁻⁷; multiplying by 60 gives 2.16.

q: Which of these is a source of random error in a set of readings?
o: A zero error in a screw gauge
A stopwatch that always runs slow
A metre rule whose zero end is worn away
Small unpredictable changes in room temperature while the readings are taken
x: Random errors vary unpredictably from reading to reading, like small fluctuations in the surroundings, and they scatter readings on both sides of the true value. The other three shift every reading the same way, so they are systematic errors.

q: A piece 12.3 ± 0.1 cm long is cut from a rod 20.5 ± 0.2 cm long. The length left over, with its uncertainty, is:
x: 20.5 − 12.3 = 8.2 cm, and when quantities are subtracted their absolute uncertainties still add: 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 cm. Subtracting the uncertainties as well gives the tempting ± 0.1 cm.

q: A runner covers 100.0 ± 0.5 m in 20.0 ± 0.2 s. The percentage uncertainty in the average speed calculated from these is:
x: Percentage uncertainties: distance 0.5/100 × 100 = 0.5 %, time 0.2/20 × 100 = 1 %. For a quotient they add, giving 1.5 %. Adding the absolute uncertainties 0.5 + 0.2 gives the wrong 0.7 %.

q: The period of a pendulum is calculated from T = 2π√(l/g), with g taken as exact. If the length l is measured with a 4 % uncertainty, the percentage uncertainty in T is:
x: T ∝ l^½, so the percentage uncertainty in T is ½ × 4 % = 2 %. Copying the 4 % unchanged, or doubling it to 8 % as for a square, are the usual slips.

q: The resistivity of a wire is found from ρ = RA/l, where A = πd²/4. R has a 2 % uncertainty, the diameter d a 1 % uncertainty and the length l a 1 % uncertainty. The percentage uncertainty in ρ is:
x: ρ = πRd²/(4l), so the percentage uncertainty is 2 % + 2 × 1 % + 1 % = 5 %. Forgetting that d is squared gives 4 %.

q: Five readings of a time are 2.4 s, 2.6 s, 2.5 s, 2.7 s and 2.3 s. Taking the mean deviation as the uncertainty, rounded to one significant figure, the result is:
x: Mean = 12.5/5 = 2.5 s. Deviations are 0.1, 0.1, 0, 0.2 and 0.2 s; their mean is 0.6/5 = 0.12 ≈ 0.1 s. Taking the largest deviation gives ± 0.2 s; the total of the deviations gives ± 0.6 s.

q: Four students record the length of the same rod. Which recorded value was measured with the greatest precision?
x: Precision depends on the smallest division (absolute uncertainty) of the instrument; 12.346 cm is recorded to 0.001 cm, the finest of the four. 12 cm, to the nearest centimetre, is the least precise.

q: The true value of g is 9.8 m s⁻². A student's five readings are 8.52, 8.51, 8.53, 8.52 and 8.52 m s⁻². These readings are:
x: The readings agree closely with one another (spread about 0.01 m s⁻²), so they are precise, but all lie far from 9.8 m s⁻², so they are not accurate; a systematic error is likely. Mixing up the two words gives the reverse answer.

q: The side of a square tile is measured as 3.0 cm. Its area, written to the correct number of significant figures, is:
x: 3.0 has two significant figures, so the area 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0 cm² keeps two. Writing 9 cm² drops a significant figure; 9.00 cm² claims more precision than the measurement has.

q: A rope measured as 7.0 m long is cut into exactly 3 equal pieces. The length of each piece, written to the correct number of significant figures, is:
x: The 3 is an exact count, so it does not limit the significant figures; the result keeps the two of 7.0 m: 7.0/3 = 2.33… → 2.3 m. Treating 3 as a one-figure measurement gives the tempting 2 m.

q: A rectangle measures 12.5 cm by 4.0 cm. Its perimeter and its area, each written to the correct number of significant figures, are:
x: Perimeter = 2(12.5 + 4.0) = 33.0 cm: in addition the answer keeps one decimal place, as the data do (the 2 is exact). Area = 12.5 × 4.0 = 50 cm², limited to two significant figures by 4.0, so 5.0 × 10¹ cm². Dropping the final zero of the perimeter is the common slip.

q: A mass of 0.00340 kg is converted to grams. Correctly written, it is:
x: 0.00340 kg = 3.40 g. Changing units does not change the number of significant figures: 0.00340 has three (the leading zeros do not count, the trailing zero does), so 3.40 g. Dropping the trailing zero gives 3.4 g.

q: The dimensions of power are:
x: Power = work/time = [ML²T⁻²]/[T] = [ML²T⁻³]. [ML²T⁻²] is energy, the slip of forgetting to divide by time.

q: In Newton's law of gravitation, F = Gm₁m₂/r². The dimensions of G are:
x: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂) = [MLT⁻²][L²]/[M²] = [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]. Multiplying by one mass instead of dividing gives [ML³T⁻²]; using r instead of r² gives [M⁻¹L²T⁻²].

q: p is the momentum and K the kinetic energy of a body. The quantity p²/K has the dimensions of:
x: p² = [M²L²T⁻²] and K = [ML²T⁻²], so p²/K = [M], a mass; indeed K = p²/2m gives p²/K = 2m. Inverting the ratio gives [M⁻¹].

q: The speed v of a wave on a stretched string depends only on the tension F and the mass per unit length μ of the string. Dimensional analysis gives:
x: Let v = kFᵃμᵇ: [LT⁻¹] = [MLT⁻²]ᵃ[ML⁻¹]ᵇ. T: −2a = −1, so a = ½; M: a + b = 0, so b = −½; L check: a − b = 1. So v ∝ √(F/μ). Swapping the signs of the powers gives √(μ/F).

q: For a real gas, (p + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, where p is the pressure and V the volume. The dimensions of the constant a are:
x: Only like quantities can be added, so a/V² has the dimensions of pressure: a = pV² = [ML⁻¹T⁻²][L⁶] = [ML⁵T⁻²]. Dividing by V² instead of multiplying gives [ML⁻⁷T⁻²]; [L³] is the dimension of b.

q: h is Planck's constant and p a momentum. The quantity h/p has the dimensions of:
x: h = [ML²T⁻¹] and p = [MLT⁻¹], so h/p = [L], a length (it is the de Broglie wavelength). Remembering h as energy × time can mislead students into answering time.
